The statement that the pH-matched intradermal comparison did not include procaine is correct.

The full text of Wightman and Vaughan 1976 adds a third and the earliest such measurement, and it matches every element: humans, procaine, intradermal wheals, discomfort on injection rated on a stated scale, randomised and double-blind within subject. It also bears on the Morris/Prien disagreement the current reason records, because procaine was neither least nor most uncomfortable here. The verdict was already refuted and stays refuted; what changes is that the refutation now rests on three studies rather than two, with the earliest predating both.

proposed_wording: Two controlled datasets on intracutaneous ester exposure exist and they point in different directions on local reactions: Weinschenk 2017 observed no type-1 allergy across intracutaneous injections of procaine, lidocaine, mepivacaine or saline, reading the larger procaine wheals as vasodilatation; and Wightman and Vaughan 1976 (PMID 791022), a randomised double-blind within-subject study in 20 volunteers, recorded localised itching, erythema and pseudopod formation after procaine in eight of 20 subjects and in no subject given any of the other five solutions.

Wightman and Vaughan 1976 matches every element: humans, procaine given intracutaneously, a controlled design (randomised, double-blind, each subject his own control), and a local-reaction outcome with concurrent non-ester and saline comparators. It is smaller than Weinschenk and was not at scale, so 'at scale' still separates them, which is why the verdict stays narrowed rather than becoming refuted. The direction matters more than the count: the page reads a single reassuring dataset as showing the ester group's measured record is better than its reputation, and the second controlled dataset on the same route reports a local-reaction rate for procaine and for no other solution tested.

quote: In contrast to saline solution alone, saline solution with benzyl alcohol gave good anesthesia for 2 minutes.
proposed_wording: Of the drug adjuvants considered here, none is both measured in a plain intradermal wheal and free of a vasoconstrictor mechanism; benzyl alcohol, the one additive that is, is a weak anaesthetic in its own right rather than a modifier, and that has been measured intradermally in humans twice: as an addition to lidocaine (Williams and Howe 1994) and on its own in saline, where it gave short-lived anaesthesia and the least discomfort on injection of six solutions in 20 volunteers (Wightman and Vaughan 1976, PMID 791022).
reason: The claim is already refuted on the strength of the benzyl alcohol trial the page itself cites. Wightman and Vaughan 1976 strengthens the characterisation the refutation rests on rather than changing the verdict: it measured benzyl alcohol in saline, timed by pin prick, in a randomised double-blind within-subject design, and found anaesthesia that began to dissipate within a few minutes. That is a second, earlier human intradermal measurement of a non-vasoconstrictor additive, and it establishes from measurement rather than inference that benzyl alcohol acts as an anaesthetic of its own.

The full text adds a second, earlier human intradermal measurement of benzyl alcohol, this time of the substance alone rather than as an addition, with both the discomfort and the duration outcomes recorded.
